title: Chapter 136 – The Standard Weights
html:
[The Court – Lin Jian]

The Court has a room where it keeps the truth, and it is a very ordinary room.

Jian sees it for the first time in the autumn of his fifty-first year, at the bottom of a spiral stair under the oldest wing of the Court Archive, three hundred paces below the capital's busiest street. Above him the city roars: carts, hawkers, the endless clatter of ten thousand clerks. Down here there is only dust, and silence, and the faint sweet smell of very old paper. A single lantern swings from the hand of the man in front of him, throwing shadows that jump along walls of gray brick.

"This is the Hall of Standard Weights," says Cheng Yun.

He is sixty-nine now, a stooped, brisk, balding man in the black robe of the Court bench, with ink on his cuffs and a limp from an old knife wound. He has been Chief Examiner for eleven years and Chief Justice for six. He is the only honest judge Jian has ever met, and he has not once in thirty years mentioned that he risked his career to save a boy from a rigged trial.

"I was sworn to secrecy," he says, over his shoulder. "I was told it held the master standard. The Court's brass weights, the great rod, the original measure of the realm. A room that would be a disaster if it were opened." He chuckles dryly. "They were not lying. They simply did not say what kind of standard."

"How long have you known?"

"Since the day you asked me about Article 44." He turns the corner. "I have been looking for the hinge ever since."

"And you found it."

"I found a door that does not open." He stops before a plain iron-bound wooden door at the end of the passage, and holds up the lantern. "Fourteen of my predecessors sat in this chair. Fourteen swore never to enter. I have broken that oath once, last winter, to look." His face is grave. "It is the only thing I have ever done in my life that I truly regret. Not because of what I saw. Because of how afraid I was to want more."

Jian lays his palm on the door.

It is warm.

* * *

He had come to the capital the way a man comes to a doctor: late, with excuses.

It had taken sixty days. He had left the Garden in the first week of the new year, with Qinghe on the porch in her lined cloak, one hand raised in a salute that was half a scolding, and Wenyuan beside her in his gloves, silent, with the baby name unspoken between them. Feng had walked him to the ford. Yue had given him a satchel of travel bread and a folded sheet of paper with the Garden's schedule of watches, in case he forgot that his house was behind him. Hu had pressed a new set of tools into his hands, a pocket vise and a set of awls, and said, gruffly, that the ones he carried were a disgrace.

The road east was wide and gray and well kept. It ran through the plain of the Three Rivers, between fields of millet and rice and long lines of poplars, past inns and ferries and market towns, and on the fifty-third day the horizon thickened into a smear of smoke, and the smoke became roofs, and the roofs became walls. The capital was a great brown city of a million souls, built on a bend of a yellow river, with towers of baked brick and a hundred bridges. It stank. It roared. A man could not walk three paces without being offered tea, tin spoons, prophecies or a good price on a goose.

Behind him, in the crowded street, the Unkept walked in single file, twelve gray figures in rags, their eyes fixed on the middle distance. The crowd parted for them as water parts for a stone. A child pointed. A mother pulled the child away. A beggar on a doorstep looked up at the white-eyed man at the head of the line, and said, wonderingly, "You're Hao's brother."

The white-eyed man stopped.

It was the first time in his life, so far as anyone knew, that a stranger had called him by a name.

"I am sorry?" he said, in his rusty voice.

"Hao. Lan Hao's brother. From the dyers' quarter." The beggar squinted. "No, he'd be a young man, wouldn't he. You must be the other one. The one they took." He rubbed his chin. "Your mother kept your shoes by the door for thirty years. Wouldn't let anyone move them."

The white-eyed man did not move. A long, silent moment passed in the roaring street. Then he sat down on the cobbles, quite slowly, in the middle of the traffic, and covered his face with his hands.

They waited with him for an hour. Nobody complained. When at last he rose, his cheeks were wet, and he said in a very small voice that his name was Lan Wen, and that he had a sister, and that she lived in the dyers' quarter, and would anyone mind terribly if he went to see her.

* * *

On the night before the descent, Cheng Yun feeds him in the judge's house in the lawyers' quarter, a narrow old building of dark timber with a courtyard and a persimmon tree, in a dining room hung with scrolls of the Court's oldest statutes.

His wife is dead. His son is a magistrate in the south. His granddaughter, a grave round-faced girl of eleven named Cheng Mei, serves the soup and watches Jian with the unblinking attention of a child who has been told that the guest is important. She sets a spoon beside his bowl. It is a plain wooden spoon, much worn.

He stares at it.

"It was my mother's," says Cheng Yun, following his eyes. "I thought you might like to use it. Your mother wrote to me last year, to ask whether the Court still had the old register of the Orchard. She said she was keeping a spoon for you." The judge smiles. "I confess I did not know what she meant. But I understood that she would be glad if you ate with one."

He eats with it. The soup is salt and bean curd and ginger, and he tastes every drop.

"You have not asked me about the Archive," says Cheng Yun, when the girl has gone to bed.

"I thought you would tell me in your own time."

"I would like to tell you now." The old man folds his hands on the table. "I have been Chief Justice six years. I have sat on every case that touched the Registry. I have signed the warrant for every inquest into a vanished man. And in every case, without exception, the file was missing. A clerk had lost it. A fire had burned it. The witness had died. I used to think it was incompetence." He lifts his eyes. "It was never incompetence. It was a hand. It reached into the Court and removed whatever it wished, and nobody noticed, because nobody remembered that it had been there."

"Article 44."

"Article 44 is the hand's fingerprint." Cheng Yun's voice is steady. "I have decided that I will not be afraid of it. I am sixty-nine. I have a granddaughter. I have a persimmon tree. If the Court cannot protect the thing beneath it, then the Court does not deserve to stand." He rises, stiffly. "I will take you down at dawn. I will unlock the door myself. And if anything comes for it, it will have to come through me."

Jian looks at him across the lamp. He cannot find a thing to say. In the end he only bows, as low as he can, over the wooden spoon and the empty bowl, and stays that way until the judge gently tells him to sit.

The Hall is smaller than the Quiet School's, and older, and wrong.

He knows it the moment he steps over the sill. The air tastes of rust and cold water. The walls are the dark green stone of the Gate, but they have been plastered over, centuries ago, and papered with hundreds of yellowed sheets of law, statutes, edicts, minutes, treaties, piled one over another like leaves on a forest floor. The lamp is the same pale brass. The desk is the same plain wood. But the room has been used.

There are shelves of ledgers. There is a rack of brass weights, rank on rank, from a grain to a ton. There is a long wooden rod, polished by centuries of hands, lying in a cradle of green felt. There is a chair, a very worn chair, with the cushion flattened to a board.

And on the wall above the desk, in letters a foot high, cut deep into the stone and gilded, are two words.

ARTICLE FORTY-FOUR.

"So it was never a law," says Jian slowly.

"It was always a law." Cheng Yun stands at his shoulder, and his voice is very quiet. "It is the oldest law in the Court. I have the text, now. I have read it forty times." He recites, as if from a lesson learned by heart. "No inquiry shall be made, by any officer of the realm, into the nature or the use of the room beneath the Archive. The room shall be kept. The room shall be guarded. The room shall be forgotten. Any officer who learns its purpose shall be held to have no oath that can bind him."

"No oath that can bind him."

"It is a very clever clause. It tells every judge that if he breaks the law, the law cannot punish him. Only his own conscience can. And so fourteen men, one after another, have walked past that door for four hundred years without a single guard on it." Cheng Yun smiles without humor. "Whoever wrote it understood us better than we understood ourselves."

Jian looks at the chair. At the desk. At the faded blue handwriting on a slip of paper left in the exact center of the blotter, under a smooth black stone.

To whoever comes after.

"Who wrote it?" asks the judge.

"The second Operator," says Jian. "I think."

* * *

He wakes the Dock with the bell.

It is the third time, and he does not enjoy it. He sits at the desk with his eyes shut and his hand flat on the wall and the little silver bell on its red thread laid in his palm, and listens, as he has listened before, for the seam. This one is closer. The Garden is only nine hundred li away; the channel is wider, the latency shorter. It takes him an hour.

```
DOCK — ARK-2
Status: DARK
Wake: 30 CE (carry cell 12)
Remote draw: 18 CE via bell seam (Reservoir 134/200)
Memory: one memory per draw. The Door chooses.
Alternative: Door-fed, Seal -6% (now 60 → 54)
Cole door closes below 60.
```

He reads it. He does not hesitate.

Draw.

The cold line runs down the back of his skull. A brightness, snuffed. CE floods into the cell, eighteen units, and the pale brass lamp lights with a soft gold flame.

Cheng Yun is watching him with a worried frown. "You look pale."

"I am well."

"What did it cost?"

Jian opens his eyes. He goes through the drawer slowly, item by item, the way a man checks his pockets in a crowd. His mother. His father. The Garden. The Orchard roll. The hoe. The spoon. The star he lost, the name of a girl he never knew. Qin Hao's token, in his breast. Bai's cane, Bai's stool, Bai's jar of dried plums.

Bai's voice.

It is simply gone. He can see the old man's face, the thick lenses, the gray tufts. He can hear the words, the dry, irritable, loving words, written in his memory like a script. You were the worst apprentice I ever had. But they are only words. The voice that spoke them has fallen out of the world like a stone from a pocket.

"It took Bai's voice," he says.

"I am sorry."

"He is not here to mind." His own voice shakes. "I would have liked to keep it."

Cheng Yun lays a hand on his shoulder, briefly. He is not a demonstrative man. He says nothing more. They stand together in the light of the golden flame, and the dust of four hundred years drifts down through it like snow.

* * *

To whoever comes after:

My name is Ethan Cole. I am the second Operator. I will not tell you how long I have been here, because it is shameful.

I am not a good man. I want you to know that at the start. I came to this Dock and I found the Gate and I was told what it was for, and I did what I think a great many people would have done. I tried to burn it down.

I was the angriest of us. I was a lawyer, I think, in the first world. I do not remember much. I remember that I was good at finding the clause that undid the contract. I found one. It took me three years.

Jian reads in the light of the gold flame, standing, with the judge at his shoulder. The log is shorter than the others. Twenty pages. The handwriting is quick, hard, slanted forward, a man who writes as he argues. He does not draw cartoons. He does not tell jokes. He numbers his points.

1. The Gate is a copying surface. It copies the Operator.

2. Copying requires a source. The source is the stored copy, in the first world. I do not know where.

3. Copying requires a medium. The medium is people.

He stops.

"Medium," says Cheng Yun.

"Names," says Jian. His mouth is very dry. He turns the page.

I did not understand it until the thirty-first night, when the Keeper came. Not the veiled woman. A man, a clerk, a Number, who had been sent to bring me wine. He was weeping. I asked him why. He said he had burned his name that morning, and could not remember it. I asked him what a Number was. He said, "A Number is a name given to the Gate."

I said, "What does the Gate do with it?"

He said, "It uses it."

That was when I understood. The Gate does not copy for free. A copy takes substance. And the substance is names. Four thousand and some, held in the Roll, burned in ceremonies, one at a time, to keep the surface warm. When the Operator is ready to go home, the Gate draws on them all at once. The whole Roll goes dark. Four thousand names are unwritten in an hour.

I was horrified. I had thought of the Gate as a machine. It is a feast.

I made a plan.

* * *

The plan is simple, and it fails.

He reads it in the cold gold light, page by page, with a growing weight in his chest. The second Operator had gone to the Court. He had found a young judge who believed him, and together they had written a law, Article 44, to hide the Dock and keep it from the Order's reach, and a second law, Article 45, which has since been removed from the books, to forbid the burning of names. For eleven years it held. The Order, caught off guard, retreated to the ridge. The Numbers, for a time, went unfed. The Gate grew cold.

Then they struck back, writes the second Operator. They were patient. They always are. They did not attack me. They attacked the judge.

I will not describe what they did. I will say only that on the morning I came to the Court, his chair was empty, his name was struck from the rolls, and nobody in the building remembered that he had ever lived. Not a clerk. Not a servant. Not his daughter.

They had burned his name.

They had made him a Number, and then they had made him nothing.

I understood, then, that the Order is not an enemy I can fight. It is not even an organization. It is an appetite, six hundred years old, with a single purpose: to see the Operator home. They believe it to be a kindness. They believe it with their whole hearts. Every name they burn, they burn to bring me back. And I cannot stop them, because if I destroy the Order, I destroy the people who are trying, in their way, to save me.

I have decided to go through. I am tired.

But before I go I will leave you one weapon. It is not much. It is the only one I found.

Names.

Return the names.

Jian lowers the page.

The room is very quiet. The gold flame stands straight and steady above the wick. Cheng Yun is breathing hard.

"The scroll," says the judge. "The one Ye Sutra-Keeper holds. The four thousand."

"She has read twelve hundred." His voice is hoarse. "I thought it was a kindness. I thought it was a way to bring people home."

"It is a weapon."

"It is a siege." He looks up. "Every name she reads aloud, the Gate loses a stone from its foundation. When the Roll runs dry, the Gate cannot be opened. It cannot be completed. It cannot restore." He swallows. "The Second House knows. They have known for years. That is why they are rising now."

* * *

The pantry opens in the dark behind the rack of brass weights.

It is a crack in the plaster no wider than a hair, hidden behind a stack of ledgers, and the Door finds it at once. He steps through. Seven jars, as before: squat, black-waxed, heavy, each with its brass tag. The fifth is gone. The fourth is gone. The second is on the shelf in front of him, cold and glowing faintly, with a creased slip of paper beneath.

This is the only one that should not be opened until you are ready.

It is a Seed. Do not plant it in your belly. Plant it in your Seal.

—E.C.

He lifts it. Beneath the slip, folded small, lies a second sheet, thin and crisp, covered in neat columns.

```
CORE SEED METHOD — GOLDEN CORE (recovered)
Prerequisite: Purple Mansion PEAK (all three tracks)
Catalyst: Jar 2 (Hollow Gold) [HELD]
Medium: The Seal (soul-vessel stabilizer, ≥ 80%)
Duration: 14 years
Cost: Seal consumed (≥ 40 points)
Reservoir: one decade of draws (~100 CE)
Memory: unknown
Warning: The Core is built from the Seal.
The Seal is the Cole door's anchor.
After the Core, the door cannot be closed.
```

He reads it standing, with the jar cradled in both arms like a sleeping child. After the Core, the door cannot be closed. He reads it twice. Behind him, Cheng Yun clears his throat.

"I am a judge," he says. "I read contracts for a living. Allow me an observation." He taps the sheet. "This is not a recipe. It is a bargain. The kind where the small print is the whole of the thing."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"I think so." He folds the paper and puts it in his breast, beside the spoon. "It means that if I do this, I cannot go back. The Door stays open. The Gate stays open. Whatever is on the other side stays open, with me on this side, and no way to shut either."

"And if you do not do it?"

"Then I never reach the Core. I never reach Nascent Soul. I never live long enough to find out." He shrugs, a little helplessly. "There are only two doors in this room, Judge. One of them has a lock on it. The other does not."

Cheng Yun regards him. He is a very old man, with a very tired face, and in his eyes is something that Jian has seen only once before, in a gray stair, on the face of Qin Hao.

"Then I will keep the one with the lock," says the judge. "For as long as I live. Nobody will enter this room unless I say so. I have the authority." A dry smile. "I have, after all, no oath that can bind me."

* * *

The Dock keeps him four days, and he spends them as he spent the others: one page at dawn, one meal at noon, one long dark silence at dusk.

Cheng Yun brings food. Pebble, who has not spoken since the stair, sits on the desk and listens to the walls. The Unkept wait in the street above under the eye of the Court guard, who have given up trying to move them. On the second evening Jian sits alone in the golden lamplight with the second Operator's last page in his hands, and reads it for the ninth time, and understands, slowly, that the man who wrote it was not angry at all.

I was never angry, the page says. I was ashamed. It is a very different thing.

I understood, at the end, that I had been afraid of the Gate because it was the only thing in the world that loved me. It wished me home. It had waited six hundred years. It was prepared to burn four thousand people to do it. And I could not forgive that, because I knew that if the choice had been mine, I would have done the same.

I do not know which of us is the monster.

He puts the page down. In the corner, Pebble lifts her head.

"I can hear her," she says.

"Who?"

"The one he was ashamed of." The little beast's eyes are enormous. "She is very old. She is in the walls. She is singing." A pause. "It is not a song for the dead. It is a song for the sleeping."

* * *

They are halfway up the spiral stair when the bell on the Archive's great tower begins to ring.

It is not a signal. It is an alarm. Jian knows the sound; it is the same as the one that rang the night the Registry struck the Gate. He and Cheng Yun look at each other. Then they are running, two gray men, one with a limp, up three hundred paces of worn stone.

They burst out into the Archive's great hall. It is empty. The clerks have fled. The long rows of desks stand deserted, the lamps burning, a half-written ledger open on the nearest. At the far end, in the doorway, framed against the white glare of the street, stands a single tall figure.

It wears a veil.

It is a plain veil of plum-colored gauze, falling from a gray hood to the breast, and beneath it Jian can make out no features at all. The figure is tall, straight-backed, still. A long narrow sword hangs at its hip. And around it, in the street, in perfect silence, stand two rows of men in gray tunics with plum-colored seals at the collar. Fifty, perhaps. They do not move. They do not carry weapons.

They simply breathe, in unison, and the air in the great hall grows thick and heavy.

"The Warden of the Roll," says Cheng Yun, under his breath. "I have heard of him."

The figure inclines its head. Its voice, when it comes, is dry, level, courteous, and not at all the voice of a man Jian knows.

"Keeper," it says. "The Roll asks for you."

"I am not the Keeper."

"You are. By recognition, by the will of the House." A faint pause. "I regret to say that I must insist."

"On what?"

"That you come home." The veiled head tilts. "The ninth is dead."

Jian's heart stops.

"She went at dawn," says the Warden. "The root was not enough. It never was. We held her as long as we could. The Chain has lost its fifth link in fifty years, and its first in a decade." The voice is quiet, almost gentle. "The eleventh has fifteen years, Keeper. After her, the Head. We cannot hold them. Only you can."

A long silence. In the dim hall, the lamps flicker. The breath of fifty men fills the air, slow and heavy and patient, like the sea.

"Fifteen years," says Jian.

"Fifteen."

"And if I come?"

"Then the Chain will be released." The Warden's hand rests lightly on the hilt of the sword. "In whatever manner you choose."

"And if I do not?"

The veil does not move. But from somewhere behind it comes a very faint sound, like a breath drawn through clenched teeth, and Jian understands, quite suddenly, that the man beneath it is not threatening him. He is begging.

"Then they will die," says the Warden. "One at a time. In their sleep. And I will stand beside each of them and watch."
